Ordering Physician: Dr. John Smith, MD Clinical Practice: Metropolis Oncology Associates Address: 456 Cancer Care Plaza, Metropolis, USA 12345 Phone: (123) 555-0123
Gross Description:
The specimen is received in formalin, labeled with the patient's name and medical record number, and designated "left breast core biopsy." It consists of three tan-white, cylindrical tissue fragments, ranging in length from 1.2 cm to 1.5 cm and in diameter from 0.2 cm to 0.3 cm. The entire specimen is submitted in one cassette.
Microscopic Description:
Histologic sections reveal cores of breast tissue with an infiltrative neoplasm. The tumor cells are arranged in irregular nests and single files, infiltrating the fibrous stroma. The neoplastic cells are pleomorphic with enlarged, hyperchromatic nuclei and prominent nucleoli. Mitotic figures are frequently identified. There is associated ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS), solid type, with high-grade nuclear features. No evidence of lymphovascular invasion is identified in the submitted material.
Diagnosis:
Invasive Ductal Carcinoma, Grade 3 of 3.
Comments:
The histomorphologic features are those of a high-grade invasive ductal carcinoma. Correlation with imaging findings and clinical presentation is recommended. Further evaluation for hormone receptor status and HER2/neu expression is pending and will be reported in an addendum.

You have undergone a colonoscopy, a diagnostic procedure in which a flexible, lighted tube was used to examine the lining of your large intestine (colon). The sedation you received for the procedure will continue to affect your judgment and coordination for the rest of the day. For your safety, it is essential that you carefully follow these instructions.
Immediate Post-Procedure Care
Transportation: You must be discharged into the care of a responsible adult who will drive you home. You are not permitted to drive, take a taxi or rideshare alone, or use public transportation by yourself.
Rest and Supervision: A responsible adult must stay with you for the remainder of the day and night. It is important to rest at home for the rest of today.
Dietary Guidelines
Begin by drinking clear liquids (such as water, apple juice, ginger ale, or broth) once you are home.
If you tolerate clear liquids well, you may advance to a light meal a few hours later. Good choices include soup, toast, crackers, or yogurt.
(a) Normal Colon
(b) Colon
Impressions:
Normal Colonoscopy: The entire colon, from the cecum to the rectum, was visualized and appeared normal. There were no polyps, masses, diverticula, or evidence of inflammation.
Activity: You may feel tired and bloated for the rest of the day. It is important to rest. Do not drive, operate machinery, or make any important decisions for at least 24 hours. You must have a responsible adult stay with you for the remainder of the day. You may resume normal activities tomorrow.
Diet: You may resume your normal diet as tolerated. Start with clear liquids and light foods (e.g., soup, gelatin, crackers) and advance to a regular diet if you are not experiencing nausea or significant bloating. Avoid heavy, greasy, or spicy foods for the first 24 hours.
Follow-up: Based on the normal findings of your colonoscopy, your next routine screening colonoscopy is recommended in 10 years. We will send a reminder to you at that time. If you experience any severe abdominal pain, persistent nausea or vomiting, fever, or significant rectal bleeding, please contact our office immediately or go to the nearest emergency room.

Clinical History: 30-year-old female with an abnormal Pap test result of Low-Grade Squamous Intraepithelial Lesion (LSIL) and positive for high-risk HPV. 
Diagnosis: Cervix, 6 o'clock, Biopsy: High-Grade Squamous Intraepithelial Lesion (CIN 2). 
Gross Description: Received in formalin, labeled "cervix 6 o'clock," are two fragments of tan-white mucosal tissue, each measuring approximately 0.3 cm. Submitted entirely in one cassette. The stromal-epithelial junction is well-defined.
